notes.breaded_vegetables:
This block spans many distinct vegetables (onion, mushroom, cauliflower, eggplant, squash, tomato, green bean, broccoli, okra, yuca, pickle, sweet potato, ...) prepared several different ways (plain battered/breaded, tempura, pakora, ...) -- a generic 'is this a fried/breaded vegetable?' attribute can't tell a true match from a false one on its own, since it's True for nearly every in-block record regardless of which vegetable it actually is. Two records should only be scored as a likely match if they agree on the specific vegetable, not just the preparation style -- propose a categorical attribute (e.g. vegetable_type) whose categories are the actual vegetable names, grounded in this block's own samples/candidate_terms, rather than (or in addition to) boolean attributes about preparation style alone.
Verified this matters in practice on this exact block: before this guidance existed, the top-scoring predicted match was 'Vegetable tempura' <-> 'Vegetable pakora' at 0.87 -- two different dishes that only share a generic 'fried vegetable' style, not a specific vegetable identity. After adding a vegetable_type categorical attribute, the top match became 'Fried onion rings' <-> real onion-ring products (0.88-0.99, vegetable_type agreeing on 'onion' both sides), and pakora/tempura stopped outscoring genuine same-vegetable matches.
PREPARATION STYLE (plain battered/breaded vs. tempura vs. pakora) is a SEPARATE, genuinely orthogonal axis from vegetable identity, not a near-synonym of vegetable_type to be pruned away -- the same vegetable can appear in more than one style (e.g. 'onion pakora' vs. 'breaded onion rings' are both onion, but not the same dish), so it carries real, independent discriminating signal and should be kept ALONGSIDE vegetable_type, not folded into it or dropped just because both attributes happen to agree on some records. Verified real regression this caused: after a revision round correctly dropped is_sweet_potato/is_onion_ring (those genuinely are just single categories of vegetable_type restated as booleans -- Cramer's V 0.87-0.95 with it, correctly redundant) it ALSO dropped is_pakora, which was never flagged as correlated with anything, leaving vegetable_type as the block's only attribute. vegetable_type alone is genuinely discriminative (71% agreement on true pairs vs. 14% on decoy pairs) but that was not enough once the blocking rule was widened to ~665 OFF records: holdout precision fell to ~5% (2/43 predictions correct), because many wrong-vegetable matches had no second attribute left to be checked against. Don't let a preparation-style attribute get pruned on the assumption vegetable_type alone covers it -- check whether it was actually flagged as correlated before dropping it, not just categorized as 'another sub-type boolean' by analogy to ones that were.
PREFER TWO SEPARATE BOOLEANS (is_tempura, is_pakora) OVER ONE preparation_style CATEGORICAL for this axis specifically -- verified real cause of a further regression: a preparation_style categorical (battered_breaded/tempura/pakora) alongside vegetable_type meant splink_model.train's two-attribute EM strategy blocked each attribute's own training pass on the OTHER attribute's exact match; on this block's small size (12-21 FNDDS records) that pass's training pool fragmented enough (few records sharing the exact same specific vegetable AND the exact same one of three prep-style values) to converge to an unstable, label-switched fit for BOTH attributes in the same round, which the loop then had to catch and drop one of them just to avoid crashing on zero comparisons. 'battered_breaded' is also the block's overwhelming majority case (tempura/pakora are the minority, distinctive styles), so it doesn't need its own explicit category -- is_tempura=False AND is_pakora=False already implies plain battered/breaded by elimination. Two boolean attributes, each mostly False, give EM a much larger, less-fragmented dominant-class pool to train the other attribute against than a 3-way categorical split does, which should avoid the same instability while still preserving the same real discriminating signal (a true match should agree on is_tempura and agree on is_pakora, same as it should on vegetable_type).
notes.beans:
This block spans many distinct bean/legume types (kidney, pinto, black, lima, garbanzo/chickpea, navy, soy, green/string, blackeye pea...) -- a match should agree on the SPECIFIC type, not just 'both are some kind of bean'. Past rounds for this block have proposed the right idea but the wrong shape: several separate boolean attributes (is_kidney, is_pinto, is_lima, is_soy, is_green, ...), each True/False independently -- these are mutually exclusive facets of one underlying property (a product's beans are kidney OR pinto OR ..., not several at once), so modeling them as independent booleans violates Fellegi-Sunter's conditional-independence assumption (splink evaluates each comparison's contribution to the match score as if it were independent evidence, but 'is_kidney=False' and 'is_pinto=True' aren't actually independent facts here) and risks the correlation-flag check this loop already runs. Prefer ONE categorical attribute (e.g. bean_type) whose categories are the specific bean types, grounded in this block's own samples/candidate_terms, over several separate per-type booleans.

Preparation method (canned vs. dried vs. frozen) has the same problem, verified directly against this block's trained model: is_canned and is_dried were proposed as separate booleans, and both learned almost no discriminating weight (agree/disagree match-weight of roughly +0.07/-0.11 for is_canned, +0.01/-0.06 for is_dried -- compare to bean_type's +2.26/-7.23), letting canned and dried bean records match each other at the model's highest confidence (0.99) purely on bean-type/description similarity, which is exactly the kind of false match this attribute set should be preventing. Model preparation method as ONE categorical attribute too (e.g. preparation: canned/dried/frozen/other), for the same conditional-independence reason as bean_type above -- a product's beans are canned OR dried OR frozen, not several at once. Consider is_refried as a modifier to bean type and the exception to the bean type categories.

A contains_meat-style attribute (flagging bean products mixed with meat, e.g. 'pork and beans', 'beans and franks') should include pork, bacon, ham, sausage, and frank(furter) as catalog_keywords. In addition to these terms on the FNDDS side the generic term 'meat' is also used -- that's fine, an attribute's fndds_keywords and catalog_keywords don't need to be identical lists, each side should use whatever terms actually occur in that side's own text. If a product has the word vegetarian on one side it cannot have meats on the other side.
notes.yogurt: A generic 'is this fruit-flavored?' boolean can't tell a true match from a false one on its own once both records are already known to be flavored yogurts -- it's True for strawberry, blueberry, peach, etc. alike, so two records with completely different flavors can still agree on every existing attribute (is_greek, fat_level, is_fruit_flavored, is_frozen) purely by coincidence. If a match should require agreeing on the SPECIFIC flavor (not just 'flavored vs. plain'), propose a categorical attribute (e.g. flavor) whose categories are the actual flavors observed in this block's own samples (strawberry, blueberry, peach, vanilla, plain, ...), rather than (or in addition to) a single is_fruit_flavored/is_plain boolean.
